y-m-63-01.title: A limit guessed from a table: how far can we trust it?
y-m-63-01.topic: Limits of functions: left-hand and right-hand limits, and the difference between the limit value and the function value
y-m-63-01.goal: Each time the data of a table is revealed, adjust your judgment and level of confidence about the limit, and explain that the limit value is a separate question from the function value at x=2.
y-m-63-01.material: The function f is defined as f(x)=(x²−4)/(x−2) when x≠2. (Read it as 'x squared minus 4' divided by 'x minus 2'.) The value at x=2 is not given at first. The values of f(x) found with a calculator by sending x close to 2 are revealed step by step. Here the 'limit value' is the value f(x) approaches when x is different from 2 and gets endlessly close to 2.
y-m-63-01.thinking.0: Gauge the range of evidence a finite table gives
y-m-63-01.thinking.1: Understand why you must check both the left-hand and right-hand limits
y-m-63-01.thinking.2: Tell apart which part of the judgment new information changes and which part it does not change
y-m-63-01.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level within this assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have already learned limits, continuity, and differentiation of polynomial functions from Calculus I.
y-m-63-01.prereq.1: The meaning of a limit: the value the function values approach as x gets endlessly close to a
y-m-63-01.prereq.2: The meaning of continuity (comparing the limit value and the function value)
y-m-63-01.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose the judgment you can state with the evidence so far.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read the values of the revealed table up and down, and write near which number f(x) gathers as x gets closer to 2.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.hint.1: Mark separately whether the evidence you have now is about values to the left of 2 or to the right, or about f(2).
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.info:
These are the values as x approaches 2 from the side less than 2.
x | 1.9 | 1.99 | 1.999
f(x) | 3.9 | 3.99 | 3.999
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Looking only at this table, what is the most appropriate judgment about 'the limit value of f(x) as x gets endlessly close to 2'?
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.after: From the left, 3.9, 3.99, 3.999 look like they are approaching 4. Still, to say that the limit value exists, you must check that it approaches the same value from the right too.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The limit value has been settled as 4. There is no need at all to look at the right-side values.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a thought that confirmed a limit exists from the values approached from one side alone. To say a limit exists, you must check that the opposite side approaches the same value too.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The values keep getting larger, so the limit is on the side of growing without bound.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a thought that treated values getting larger and growing without end as the same. Look at whether the values get close to some number without exceeding it.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: From the left it seems to approach 4. We must look at the right too.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a thought that states the trend the one-sided data shows while separating how far the evidence goes and putting off the judgment.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We can't know the value at x=2, so we can't talk about the limit either.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: A limit looks at the change when x is different from 2, so you can talk about it even if you don't know f(2). This is a thought that mixes the function value and the limit value.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.info:
These are the values as x approaches 2 from the side greater than 2.
x | 2.1 | 2.01 | 2.001
f(x) | 4.1 | 4.01 | 4.001
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: You have now seen the data from both sides. What is your judgment about the limit value now?
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.after: The guess that it gathers at 4 from both sides is reasonable. However, a table is just a few points, so your confidence grows more if you confirm that for x≠2, f(x) simplifies to x+2.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The left is 3.99… and the right is 4.01…, which differ, so there is no limit.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a thought that saw the numbers written in the table themselves as different. In a limit, you look at whether the values from both sides approach the same number.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The values in the table have never been exactly 4, so the limit value is not 4.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a thought that treated the limit value as a value that is reached exactly. The criterion is whether it gets endlessly close.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Both sides approach 4, so the limit value seems to be 4.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment that cites as grounds that the data from both sides gathers at the same number.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: A table is only grounds for a guess. I also want to simplify the expression and check that 4 is right.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that knows the limit that a table is a finite number of points and tries to raise confidence by another method.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Now the value at x=2 is known. f(2)=1.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does this new information affect the judgment about the limit value?
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.after: The limit value is the value f(x) approaches at points other than x=2, so whatever number f(2) is, it stays 4. What changes is whether the graph is connected at x=2 (whether it is continuous).
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The limit value stays 4. But the graph breaks at x=2.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a thought that separated that the limit value does not depend on the value at x=2 itself, and that the new information affects a different property (being connected).
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The limit value changes to 1 and becomes equal to the value at x=2.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a thought that read the value at x=2 as the limit value. The limit value is decided by the change at x different from 2.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The limit value 4 and f(2)=1 are different, so the limit does not exist.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a thought that treated the limit existing and its value equaling the function value as one condition.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: We can no longer know which of 4 and 1 is the limit value.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a thought that withdrew all the earlier evidence because of the new value. Think about the fact that the two values answer different questions.
y-m-63-01.s.s1.reflect: As each piece of new information came in, which judgments stayed the same and which changed? How was your level of confidence different when you guessed from a few rows of a table versus when you confirmed with a formula?
y-m-63-01.s.s2.prompt: If f(2)=1, is this function f continuous at x=2?
y-m-63-01.s.s2.hint.0: Say in words which two values must be equal for it to be continuous.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write side by side the limit value decided in the earlier step and f(2) and compare them.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.o.a: It is continuous. The value at x=2 is set by f(2)=1.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that checked only that the function value is defined and did not compare it with the limit value.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.o.b: It is continuous. The limit value 4 exists at x=2, so it does not break.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that checked only that the limit exists and did not compare it with the function value.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.o.c: It is not continuous. The limit does not exist at x=2.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that did not reflect the result from the earlier step that both limits gathered at 4.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.o.d: It is not continuous. The limit value 4 and f(2)=1 are different from each other.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.r.d: This is a judgment that used the point that comparing the limit value and the function value is the key condition of continuity.
y-m-63-01.s.s2.explain: To be continuous at x=2, the limit value must exist and equal f(2). Here the limit value is 4 and f(2)=1, which differ, so it is not continuous.
y-m-63-01.s.s3.prompt: What value would you change f(2) to so that f is continuous at x=2? Also write what the limit value becomes when you change it that way.
y-m-63-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write again the number f(x) was approaching in the table of the earlier step.
y-m-63-01.s.s3.hint.1: In light of the condition for continuity, write in one sentence what number f(2) must be.
y-m-63-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If I make f(2) ..., then ...
y-m-63-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you name a value that makes it connect, not the value (1) that makes it break at x=2?
y-m-63-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart in your own words whether the limit value changes with f(2) or not?
y-m-63-01.s.s3.model.0: If you set f(2) to 4, it becomes continuous at x=2. The limit value 4 stays the same even if you change f(2).
y-m-63-01.s.s3.model.1: You should define the function value at x=2 to equal the limit value, 4. The limit value is decided regardless of the value at 2, so it does not change.

y-m-63-02.title: If the limit of a sum exists, do the limits of each function exist too?
y-m-63-02.topic: Properties of limits of functions: the limit of a sum and counterexamples
y-m-63-02.goal: Refute the claim 'if the limit of a sum exists, the limit of each function exists' with a counterexample, and sort out in which direction the sum law of limits holds.
y-m-63-02.material: Gyuri said, "If the limit of f(x)+g(x) exists as x approaches 0, then the limit of f(x) and the limit of g(x) each exist too." Here f and g are functions defined near x=0 (x≠0). 'The limit exists' means it approaches a single real number, and cases where it grows without bound or shrinks without bound, or where the left and right differ, are called 'the limit does not exist'. 1/x is read 'one over x'.
y-m-63-02.thinking.0: Check the direction of the claim (its converse)
y-m-63-02.thinking.1: Build a counterexample with a pair of functions that cancel
y-m-63-02.thinking.2: Sort out the statements that always hold
y-m-63-02.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level within this assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have already learned limits, continuity, and differentiation of polynomial functions from Calculus I.
y-m-63-02.prereq.1: The sum law of limits (if each has a limit, the limit of the sum is the sum of the limits)
y-m-63-02.prereq.2: The fact that the limit of 1/x as x approaches 0 does not exist (it grows or shrinks without bound)
y-m-63-02.s.s1.prompt: What is the most appropriate first reaction when you first see Gyuri's claim?
y-m-63-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think of one function that grows without bound and one that shrinks without bound as x approaches 0.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write with a formula what shape you get when you add those two functions.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.o.a: It is true. The sum law of limits says exactly that.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.r.a: This is a thought that did not check that the 'assumption' and 'conclusion' of the sum law are reversed compared with the claim.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.o.b: It seems true. If the sum approaches a number, each part must also be near some number.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.r.b: This is a thought that assumed if the sum is stable, each part is stable too. It did not look at whether large values can cancel each other.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.o.c: It may be false. Even if each one gets large and small, they can cancel in the sum.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.r.c: This is a thought that does not just accept the claim but tries to find and test directly a case where cancellation occurs in the sum.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.o.d: Can't tell. We can't substitute 0, so we can't judge the limit.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.r.d: This is a thought that gave up judging because x=0 can't be substituted. There is a way to look at how the values approach.
y-m-63-02.s.s1.explain: To test whether the claim is 'always' true, the most direct way is to look for an example where the limit of the sum exists but those of the individual functions do not.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.prompt: With f(x)=a/x and g(x)=b/x+c (x≠0, and a, b, c are integers from −9 to 9), make 2 different examples where Gyuri's claim is wrong. The limit of f(x)+g(x) must exist but the limit of f must not exist.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.hint.0: Combine f(x)+g(x) into one fraction and look at what must happen to the part where x stays in the denominator for the sum to be a constant.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a nonzero value for a, and then choose b so that the part of the sum with x in the denominator disappears.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, c are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, c must be integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The limit of f(x)=a/x does not exist as x approaches 0.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.fail.c2: If a is 0, f becomes 0 and the limit exists. Then it is not a counterexample.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.ok.c3: f(x)+g(x) approaches a single number near x=0.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.fail.c3: f(x)+g(x)=(a+b)/x+c does not approach a single number near x=0. Look at the part where x stays in the denominator.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.explain: In f(x)+g(x)=(a+b)/x+c, if a+b=0 the sum is the constant c. But if a≠0, both f and g grow or shrink without bound as x approaches 0, so their limits do not exist. For example, if f(x)=1/x and g(x)=−1/x, the sum is 0 so its limit is 0, but neither has a limit individually.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.prompt: In the example you made, explain in one or two sentences what f(x) and g(x) each do as x approaches 0, and why the sum has a limit.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Check the f and g you made by the values when you plug in x=0.1 and 0.01.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what happens when you add f(x) and g(x) at the same x.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write separately the reason f and g each have no limit and the reason the sum has a limit?
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you cite the specific numbers (a, b, c) you made as grounds?
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.model.0: f(x)=1/x and g(x)=−1/x grow or shrink without bound as x approaches 0, so each has no limit. But when you add them you get 0, so the limit of the sum is 0.
y-m-63-02.s.s2.because.model.1: a/x and −a/x+c each diverge because the denominator approaches 0, but when you add the two functions, the parts with x cancel and only the constant c remains, so the sum approaches c.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.prompt: When f and g are functions defined near x=0, choose everything that always holds as x approaches 0.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.hint.0: Substitute the f and g you made in the earlier step into each statement and check whether the statement breaks.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.hint.1: For d, suppose f has a limit, and write how g is expressed if you assume f+g has a limit.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.o.a: If the limit of f+g exists, the limits of f and g each exist too.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.r.a: This is a judgment that took as true the direction going back from the limit of the sum to the limit of each part. Recall the counterexample from the earlier step.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.o.b: If the limits of both f and g exist, the limit of f+g also exists.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.r.b: This is a judgment that read the direction of the sum law of limits correctly (if each exists, the sum exists).
y-m-63-02.s.s3.o.c: If neither the limit of f nor the limit of g exists, the limit of f+g does not exist either.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.r.c: This is a judgment that if each has no limit, the sum has none either. Compare it with the earlier example where you made a cancelling pair.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.o.d: If the limit of f exists and the limit of g does not, the limit of f+g does not exist.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.r.d: This is a judgment that reasoned with g=(f+g)−f that cancellation cannot happen when only one has a limit.
y-m-63-02.s.s3.explain: b is the sum law of limits. d holds because if we assume the limit of f+g exists, then the limit of g=(f+g)−f would have to exist too, which gives a contradiction. For a and c, f=1/x and g=−1/x from the earlier step are counterexamples.

y-m-63-03.title: How many pairs (a, b) are there in all that don't break at x=1?
y-m-63-03.topic: Continuity of functions: undetermined coefficients of piecewise-defined functions
y-m-63-03.goal: Confirm by building them yourself that there are several pairs of constants that make a piecewise-defined function continuous at x=1, and judge what changes when the differentiability condition is added.
y-m-63-03.material:
For constants a and b, define the function f as follows.
For x<1, f(x)=x²+ax
For x≥1, f(x)=3x+b
(x² is read 'x squared'.) Let's find (a, b) that make this function continuous at x=1.
y-m-63-03.thinking.0: Organize the condition for continuity in words
y-m-63-03.thinking.1: Build several solutions that satisfy the constraint
y-m-63-03.thinking.2: Reason how the number of solutions changes when a condition is added
y-m-63-03.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level within this assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have already learned limits, continuity, and differentiation of polynomial functions from Calculus I.
y-m-63-03.prereq.1: The definition of continuity using the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value
y-m-63-03.prereq.2: Derivatives of polynomial functions, and the meaning of the left and right derivatives
y-m-63-03.s.s1.prompt: Which is a correct explanation of the condition needed for f to be continuous at x=1?
y-m-63-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the limit value of the left expression at x=1, the limit value of the right expression, and f(1), each in terms of a and b.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write in words what relationship the three values must have for the graph not to break at x=1.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.o.a: It is continuous at x=1 as long as f(1) is defined.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.r.a: This is a thought that saw only the function value being defined as the condition for continuity. The relationship between the limit value and the function value is missing.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.o.b: The left-hand limit and right-hand limit are the same, and that value equals f(1).
y-m-63-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a thought that translated the definition of continuity exactly as the agreement of the limits from both sides with the function value.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.o.c: The derivative values of the two expressions at x=1 must equal each other.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.r.c: This is a thought that mixed the condition for differentiability with the condition for continuity.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.o.d: The expression for x<1 and the expression for x≥1 must be the same expression.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.r.d: This is a thought that saw the two expressions needing to be the same for it to be continuous. Even if the expressions differ, they can connect as long as they meet at the same value.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.o.e: The values 1+a and 3+b, obtained by substituting x=1 into the two expressions, are equal.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.r.e: This is a thought that used the fact that both expressions of this function are polynomials, so the limit values can be found by substitution.
y-m-63-03.s.s1.explain: Continuity means (left-hand limit)=(right-hand limit)=f(1). Since both sides of this function are polynomials, writing that the values obtained by substituting x=1 into the two expressions are equal gives the same condition (1+a=3+b).
y-m-63-03.s.s1.acc.0: Both expressions are polynomials, so the substituted value is the limit value, and writing 1+a=3+b is the same condition. Check once more with the general definition (left-hand limit=right-hand limit=f(1)).
y-m-63-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different pairs (a, b) for which f is continuous at x=1. (a and b are numbers from −9 to 9)
y-m-63-03.s.s2.hint.0: Plug x=1 into the expression for x<1 and the expression for x≥1 to make two values in terms of a and b.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.hint.1: Set those two values equal, then choose a first and adjust b.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are from −9 to 9.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be from −9 to 9.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.ok.c2: At x=1, the limits from both sides and f(1) are equal.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.fail.c2: At x=1, the left-hand limit and f(1) differ, so the graph breaks. Compare the values you get by plugging x=1 into the two expressions.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.explain: The continuity condition is just one equation, 1+a=3+b, that is, a=b+2. There are two unknowns but only one equation, so if you choose a, b is determined to follow, and there are infinitely many such pairs.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences, using the relationship between a and b, why (a, b) is not determined as a single pair and many pairs were possible.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Calculate a−b for each of the three pairs you made.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write whether the calculated values are all the same, and if so, what they are.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in your own words that one equation cannot determine two unknowns?
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check one of the pairs you made by plugging it into that relationship?
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.model.0: At x=1 the values of the two expressions must be equal, so 1+a=3+b, that is, a=b+2. The condition is just this one equation, so if you choose b first, a is determined to follow, and there are many pairs.
y-m-63-03.s.s2.because.model.1: To be continuous, the difference between a and b just has to be 2. There is one equation but two unknowns, so if you choose one freely, the other is adjusted to fit, and there are many pairs.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.prompt: Now the condition that f is differentiable at x=1 has been added. Among the continuous (a, b) made earlier, what happens to those that also satisfy this condition?
y-m-63-03.s.s3.hint.0: Find the derivatives of the expression for x<1 and the expression for x≥1, plug in x=1, and compare the values.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many pairs satisfy both the new equation you got and the continuity condition a=b+2.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.o.a: All of them satisfy it. This is because if it is continuous, it must be differentiable.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.r.a: This is a thought that saw continuous as meaning differentiable. Even if it is continuous, the derivative may not exist at a bend.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.o.b: There is none. Continuity and differentiability cannot hold at the same time.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.r.b: This is a thought that saw the two conditions as mutually exclusive. There are many functions for which both properties hold together.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.o.c: There are infinitely many depending on the value of a. The differentiability condition is also the same equation as a=b+2.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.r.c: This is a thought that saw the new condition as the same equation as the earlier condition. If you calculate the left and right derivatives directly, you get a different equation.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.r.d: This is a judgment that narrowed down the solutions by adding the condition that the slopes of the left expression and the right expression must be equal at x=1.
y-m-63-03.s.s3.explain: The left derivative at x=1 is 2+a, found by plugging x=1 into (x²+ax)′, and the right derivative is (3x+b)′=3. For the two values to be equal, a=1, and from the continuity condition a=b+2, b=−1.

y-m-63-04.title: Can we find f(3) from this condition alone?
y-m-63-04.topic: Determining a polynomial function with the definition of the derivative and a limit condition
y-m-63-04.goal: From the given limit condition, sort out what can be known about the function (f(2), f′(2)), and judge what extra information is needed for f(3) to be determined.
y-m-63-04.material:
f is a polynomial function, and the following limit condition is given.
The limit value of f(x)/(x−2) as x approaches 2 is 3.
(This means the limit value of 'f(x) divided by x minus 2' is 3.) Let's look at whether the value of f(3) can be found.
y-m-63-04.thinking.0: Tell apart what the condition says and what it does not say
y-m-63-04.thinking.1: Judge whether extra information is sufficient

y-m-63-04.s.s1.prompt: What can be said about the value of f(2) under this condition?
y-m-63-04.s.s1.hint.0: Test with numbers what happens to the quotient if the numerator approaches a nonzero number as the denominator approaches 0.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.hint.1: Divide into the case where the numerator approaches 0 and the case where it does not, and compare how the quotient moves.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.r.a: This is a thought that read the limit value 3 of the quotient as f(2). 3 is the limit of the quotient of f(x) divided by x−2.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.r.b: This is a thought that missed that if the numerator approaches a nonzero number as the denominator approaches 0, the quotient grows without bound.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.r.c: This is a thought that reasoned how the numerator must move for the quotient to approach a finite number when the denominator goes to 0.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.o.d: The value of f(2) cannot be known and only f′(2) can be known.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.r.d: This is a thought that could not connect the numerator f(x)−f(2) of the difference quotient with the f(x) in this condition.
y-m-63-04.s.s1.explain: The denominator x−2 approaches 0, so for the quotient to approach 3 the numerator f(x) must also approach 0. A polynomial function is continuous, so f(2)=0, and then f(x)/(x−2)=(f(x)−f(2))/(x−2), so we can also know that f′(2)=3.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.prompt: Besides f(2)=0 and f′(2)=3, what added information would determine the value of f(3) as one? Choose everything that is sufficient.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many coefficients must be found for linear, quadratic, and cubic functions, and compare with the number of conditions you already have.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.hint.1: For each option, test whether you can make two or more functions that satisfy all the conditions.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that did not check that knowing only the degree does not determine the coefficients of a quadratic function as one.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that used the fact that a linear function is completely determined by f(2)=0 and the slope f′(2)=3.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.o.c: f is a cubic function and f(0)=−2.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that saw adding one value as determining it. A cubic function has many coefficients, so one value still leaves one coefficient.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.o.d: f is a cubic function and f(1)=−3.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.r.d: This is a judgment that saw a function as determined because it happens to match the value of one linear function. Other functions can have the same value.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.o.e: f is a quadratic function and f(0)=−2.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.r.e: This is a judgment that added the degree and one function value and matched the number of coefficients to be found with the number of conditions.
y-m-63-04.s.s2.explain: f(2)=0 and f′(2)=3 are already two conditions. A linear function has two coefficients, so it is determined as f(x)=3(x−2), and f(3)=3. If a quadratic function and f(0)=−2 are given together, it is determined as f(x)=(x−2)(x+1), and f(3)=4. The fact of being quadratic alone does not determine f(3)=p+3 (p is the coefficient of x²), and adding one value to a cubic function leaves one coefficient.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.prompt: We want to show that adding only 'f is a quadratic function' is not enough. With f(x)=ax²+bx+c (a, b, c are integers, a≠0), make 2 functions that satisfy the earlier conditions (f(2)=0, f′(2)=3) but have different f(3).
y-m-63-04.s.s3.hint.0: First choose an a, and write how b and c are determined to follow from the two conditions.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.hint.1: Make two functions with different a, and then calculate f(3) for each and compare.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.ok.c1: a is a nonzero integer, and b and c are also integers.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.fail.c1: Since it is quadratic, a must be a nonzero integer, and b and c must also be integers.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.fail.c2: f(2), found by plugging in x=2, is not 0.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.fail.c3: f(x)/(x−2) does not approach 3 as x approaches 2. Look at what expression the quotient equals when f(2)=0, and at the value of that expression when you plug in 2.
y-m-63-04.s.s3.explain: If we write f(x)=(x−2)(px+q), then f′(2)=2p+q=3, so q=3−2p, and f(3)=p+3. If p changes, f(3) changes too. For example, if f(x)=x²−x−2, then f(3)=4, and if f(x)=2x²−5x+2, then f(3)=5.

y-m-63-05.title: Hajun's differentiation, from where did it go wrong?
y-m-63-05.topic: Differentiating polynomial functions: checking errors in a solution using the product rule
y-m-63-05.goal: In a solution that finds the derivative of a function given as a product, find the line with the error, explain that having the same value at one point does not guarantee that the solution is valid, and rewrite it correctly.
y-m-63-05.material:
Hajun found the derivative f′(x) of f(x)=(x²+1)(x³−x) as follows. (x² is read 'x squared' and x³ is read 'x cubed'.)
The lines are the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th lines from the top.

y-m-63-05.thinking.1: Evaluate whether agreement at one point is enough as evidence

y-m-63-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Hajun's solution where a rule is used wrongly.

y-m-63-05.s.s1.hint.1: Apply the rule of the 3rd line to a very simple product like x·x, expand and differentiate directly, and compare the result.
y-m-63-05.s.s1.line.0: Let g(x)=x²+1 and h(x)=x³−x. Then f(x)=g(x)h(x).
y-m-63-05.s.s1.explain: The 3rd line is wrong. The derivative of the product of two functions is not g′(x)h′(x) but g′(x)h(x)+g(x)h′(x). In the simple example x·x, the product of the derivatives is 1·1=1, but the derivative of x² is 2x. Lines 1 and 2 are right, and the 4th line just calculates the result of the 3rd line as it is.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.prompt: Hajun said, "I also got 4 for f′(1) when I differentiated the expression x⁵−x, which I got by expanding the product first. My result also gave 4, so my solution is right!" Which is an appropriate judgment of this statement?
y-m-63-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one other value besides x=1, and calculate Hajun's result and the result of differentiating after expanding for it.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.hint.1: Use the fact that if two expressions are the same, they must be the same at any x.

y-m-63-05.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that saw the size of the tested point as the problem. What matters is checking at different points.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.o.b: Being the same at one point can be a coincidence. You should check at other x too.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that does not draw a conclusion from agreement at one point and tries to choose more points to test.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.o.c: Right. The same value came out with both methods, so the solution is also correct.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that saw having the same value at one point as evidence that the expressions are the same.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.o.d: Wrong. He did not use the product rule, so the values can't be the same.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.r.d: This is a judgment that mixed up the method being wrong with the values being the same at one point. A wrong method can also give the same value by coincidence.
y-m-63-05.s.s2.explain: At x=1, both happen to be 4. At x=2, Hajun's expression gives 6·8−4=44 and the expression 5x⁴−1 from differentiating after expanding gives 79, so they differ. Agreement at one point is not evidence that the expressions are the same.
y-m-63-05.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Hajun's 3rd line correctly to find the correct f′(x), and tell Hajun in one sentence what was wrong.

y-m-63-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the reason it is wrong in terms of which rule is right, not just 'the rule is different'?
y-m-63-05.s.s3.model.0: By the product rule, f′(x)=g′h+gh′=2x(x³−x)+(x²+1)(3x²−1)=5x⁴−1. You must use the product rule, not multiply the derivatives.
y-m-63-05.s.s3.model.1: If you expand first, f(x)=x⁵−x, so f′(x)=5x⁴−1. Hajun just multiplied the separate derivatives, but the derivative of a product doesn't work that way.

y-m-63-06.title: If it's continuous, is the slope determined as one value too?
y-m-63-06.topic: The relationship between continuity and differentiability (reading a difference-quotient table)
y-m-63-06.goal: Using a table near x=1 as evidence, judge a claim about the relationship between continuity and differentiability, and write out the relationship between the two properties exactly, including its direction.
y-m-63-06.material:
Look at the two functions f(x)=|x−1| (absolute value) and g(x)=(x−1)² at x=1. (|x−1| is read 'the absolute value of x minus 1' and (x−1)² is read 'x minus 1, squared'.) f(1)=0 and g(1)=0. h is a nonzero number, and the derivative at x=1 is the value that {f(1+h)−f(1)}/h approaches as h approaches 0. Jihye said, 'If a function is continuous at x=1, then that function is differentiable at x=1.'
h | −0.1 | −0.01 | 0.01 | 0.1
f(1+h) | 0.1 | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.1
{f(1+h)−f(1)}/h | −1 | −1 | 1 | 1
g(1+h) | 0.01 | 0.0001 | 0.0001 | 0.01
{g(1+h)−g(1)}/h | −0.1 | −0.01 | 0.01 | 0.1

y-m-63-06.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that read whether it is continuous from the trend of the function values.
y-m-63-06.s.s1.o.b: The average of the values of f, −1 and 1, is 0, so the derivative of f at x=1 is 0.
y-m-63-06.s.s1.r.b: This is a thought that combined different left and right values by averaging. A derivative is determined only when the values gather at one value.
y-m-63-06.s.s1.o.c: The values of f come out different, −1 and 1, so f is not continuous at x=1.
y-m-63-06.s.s1.r.c: This is a thought that read the difference quotient having different values as meaning not continuous. Whether it is continuous is seen in the values of f(1+h).
y-m-63-06.s.s1.o.d: The difference quotient of g approaches 0 from both sides, so the derivative of g appears to be 0.
y-m-63-06.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that read the left and right difference quotients gathering at the same number as grounds for the derivative.
y-m-63-06.s.s1.explain: f(1+h) approaches 0 like 0.1, 0.01, so it looks continuous, and the difference quotient of g approaches 0 from both sides, so its derivative looks like 0. The difference quotient of f differs, −1 for h<0 and 1 for h>0.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.prompt: About Jihye's claim 'if it is continuous, it is differentiable', which is the most appropriate judgment based on the table?
y-m-63-06.s.s2.hint.0: In the table of f, find the column where the evidence for continuity and the evidence for the derivative conflict.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check with the formula |h|/h whether the four values in the table have the same shape for all h.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.o.a: It is true. Both f and g are continuous at x=1, so it holds.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that checked only that there are two continuous examples and did not look at whether both are differentiable.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.o.b: It is false. g is continuous but its derivative is 0, so it is not differentiable.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that mixed up the derivative being 0 with the derivative not existing.

y-m-63-06.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that used as a counterexample a continuous function whose left and right slopes differ.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.o.d: Can't tell. There are only four values of h, so we need to look further with a formula.
y-m-63-06.s.s2.r.d: This is a careful judgment that is aware of the limit that a table is finitely many points and tries to check with a formula.

So 'if continuous, then differentiable' has a counterexample and is not true. With a formula, f(1+h)−f(1)=|h|, so the difference quotient is always 1 if h>0 and always −1 if h<0.

y-m-63-06.s.s3.model.0: If it is differentiable, it is always continuous, but being continuous does not mean it is differentiable. For example, |x−1| is continuous at x=1 but not differentiable because the left and right slopes differ.
y-m-63-06.s.s3.model.1: A differentiable function is continuous. But not every continuous function is differentiable. At a point where the graph has a sharp bend, for example x=0 of |x|, it is continuous but has no derivative.

y-m-63-07.title: Is there only one tangent line through point P?
y-m-63-07.topic: Equation of a tangent line: tangent lines drawn from a point outside the curve
y-m-63-07.goal: In the process of finding tangent lines drawn from a point not on the curve, tell apart the point of tangency and the point the line passes through, and confirm directly that there can be several possible tangent lines.
y-m-63-07.material:
There is a curve y=x² and a point P(1, −3). (Read 'y is x squared'.) When x=1, the y value of the curve is 1, so point P is not a point on the curve. Nara solved it like this.
"If f(x)=x², then f′(x)=2x and f′(1)=2. So the tangent line through point P(1, −3) with slope 2 is y−(−3)=2(x−1), that is, y=2x−5."
A tangent line is a line that passes through a point on the curve (the point of tangency) and has the derivative at that point as its slope.

y-m-63-08.title: How do we determine the velocity at a single instant?
y-m-63-08.topic: From average rate of change to instantaneous rate of change: the meaning of velocity
y-m-63-08.goal: Check the idea of determining instantaneous velocity from a table of average velocities found on shrinking intervals, and rewrite this idea in words a middle school student can understand, without limit notation.
y-m-63-08.material:
Let the distance a ride has traveled in t seconds since it started be s(t)=2t²+t (meters). (Read '2 t squared plus t'.) At t=2, s(2)=10 meters. We calculated the average velocity {s(2+h)−s(2)}/h on the interval [2, 2+h] seconds starting at 2 seconds.
h (seconds) | 1 | 0.5 | 0.1 | 0.01

y-m-63-09.title: If it's a local maximum, is it the maximum on the interval?
y-m-63-09.topic: Local extrema and the maximum on a closed interval
y-m-63-09.goal: Sort out when a local maximum equals the maximum on a closed interval and when it does not, build intervals yourself where the claim breaks, and organize what to compare to find the maximum.
y-m-63-09.material:
Consider the function f(x)=x³−3x. (Read 'x cubed minus 3x'.) The derivative is f′(x)=3(x+1)(x−1). Below are the values at integer x.
x | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3
f(x) | −2 | 2 | 0 | −2 | 2 | 18
Minji said, 'If there is a point inside a closed interval that is a local maximum, then that local maximum value is the maximum of f on that interval.'
y-m-63-09.thinking.0: Revise your judgment according to new information
y-m-63-09.thinking.1: Build intervals that serve as counterexamples according to conditions
y-m-63-09.thinking.2: Organize the candidates for the maximum without leaving any out

y-m-63-09.prereq.1: The sign of the derivative and increasing and decreasing, and the meaning of local maximum and local minimum

y-m-63-09.s.s1.prompt: Which is a correct statement about the maximum of f on the closed interval [−2, 2]?
y-m-63-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write the x where f′(x)=0 and the values of f at both ends of the interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.hint.1: Find the largest of the values you wrote, and find all the x that give that value.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.o.a: The maximum is 2, and it is taken only at x=−1, where there is a local maximum.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that looked only at the local maximum and did not compare with the values at the ends of the interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that read the smallest value as the maximum by mistake or looked only at the local minimum.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.o.c: The maximum is 2, and it is taken at x=−1 and x=2.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that gathered and compared the points that are local extrema and the values at the ends of the interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.o.d: There is no maximum. A local maximum cannot be the maximum of the interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.r.d: This is a thought that missed the case where a local maximum can equal the maximum of the interval. Compare it with the values at the ends of this interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s1.explain: There is a local maximum at x=−1 with f(−1)=2, and at the endpoints f(−2)=−2 and f(2)=2. So the maximum is 2, taken at x=−1 and x=2. On this interval, Minji's statement seems to hold.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.prompt: We widened the interval to [−2, 3], and f(3)=18. What happens to Minji's statement?
y-m-63-09.s.s2.hint.0: When the interval is [−2, 3], check whether the point that is a local maximum is still inside the interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.hint.1: Put the local maximum value and the value at the new endpoint side by side and compare which is larger.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.o.a: It does not hold. The value 18 at the endpoint x=3 is greater than 2.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that compared even the value at the endpoint newly included as the interval widened.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.o.b: It still holds. The local maximum 2 is still in the interval.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that checked only that the local maximum is in the interval and did not compare whether there is a larger value.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.o.c: It does not hold. The point that was a local maximum disappeared as the interval changed.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that missed that a local maximum is determined by the shape near x=−1, so it stays even if the ends of the interval change.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.o.d: If you change the interval it becomes a different function, so you can't compare.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.r.d: This is a judgment that missed that the function stays the same and only the interval being looked at changed.
y-m-63-09.s.s2.explain: There is a local maximum at x=−1 and the local maximum value stays 2. But at the new endpoint x=3, f(3)=18 is a larger value, so the maximum of this interval is not the local maximum but 18.
y-m-63-09.s.s3.prompt: Make 2 different closed intervals [p, q] on which Minji's statement does not hold. p and q are integers from −9 to 9, the point x=−1 that is a local maximum must be inside the interval (p<−1<q), and yet the maximum of that interval must be greater than the local maximum 2.

y-m-63-09.s.s3.fail.c3: The values of f at both ends of this interval are all at most the local maximum 2, so this is an interval where Minji's statement holds. Calculate the value of f at the endpoints.
y-m-63-09.s.s3.explain: f(x)>2 happens when f(x)−2=(x−2)(x+1)²>0, that is, x>2. If the interval includes x=−1 inside and its right end q is greater than 2, then f(q)>2, so the local maximum 2 is not the maximum of that interval.

y-m-63-10.material:
For the function f(x)=x³−6x²+9x and a real number k, find the number of distinct real roots of the equation f(x)=k (distinct real numbers x that satisfy the equation) depending on the value of k. (Read 'x cubed minus 6 x squared plus 9x'.) Below is f(x) at integer x.

f(x) | 0 | 4 | 2 | 0 | 4

y-m-63-10.prereq.1: The sign of the derivative and increasing and decreasing, and the meaning of local maximum and local minimum

y-m-63-10.s.s1.prompt: As k changes, the data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your judgment about the number of distinct real roots.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.hint.0: In the table, pair up and find the intervals where the value of f(x) goes from below k to above k, and where it goes from above to below.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.hint.1: When using the information on increasing and decreasing, check interval by interval whether the range over which f rises and falls in each interval passes through k.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.info: Consider the equation f(x)=2 for k=2. In the table, f(2)=2.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many distinct real roots do you think f(x)=2 has? (f is a continuous cubic function and has at most 3 distinct real roots.)
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Since f(0)=0<2<f(1)=4, there is a root between 0 and 1; since f(2)=2, there is a root at x=2; and since f(3)=0<2<f(4)=4, there is a root between 3 and 4. There are at most 3 distinct real roots, so there are exactly 3 (in fact 2−√3, 2, 2+√3).
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a judgment that stopped after looking at just the one root x=2 found in the table. See whether there are more intervals where the table value goes from below 2 to above 2.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that found all the intervals in the table where the value of f(x) crosses 2 and counted the places of the roots.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment that added just one to the root checked in the table. Check whether you found all the intervals where the value passes through 2.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It can't be known from the table alone.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment that saw it as impossible to say anything about x not in the table. You can use the property that when a continuous function crosses a value, there is a root in between.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.info: Consider f(x)=5 for k=5. All the f(x) in the table are at most 4. When we widened the table, f(5)=20 and f(−1)=−16. Also f′(x)=3(x−1)(x−3), so f is increasing for x<1, decreasing for 1<x<3, and increasing for x>3.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many distinct real roots does f(x)=5 have?
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.after: For x<1, f is increasing but rises only up to f(1)=4 and doesn't reach 5; for 1<x<3 it goes down from 4 to 0; and for x>3 it increases from 0, and since f(4)=4<5<f(5)=20, it passes 5 once between 4 and 5. There is 1 distinct real root.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a thought that judged by looking only at values within the range of the table. Look at how f changes outside the table.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a thought that carried over the number for k=2 as it is. When k changes, the place where the horizontal line meets the graph changes too.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a thought that carried over the number for the case of touching at a local extremum. Check whether f(x)=5 equals an extreme value.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that checked in each interval of increase and decrease whether the value of f crosses 5 and counted the places of the roots.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.2.info: The local maximum value is f(1)=4 and the local minimum value is f(3)=0. Move the horizontal line y=k up and down on the graph and count the points where it meets. When k=0 and k=4, the horizontal line touches the graph at the local extremum points.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which range of k gives exactly 3 distinct real roots?
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.2.after: If k is between 0 and 4, the horizontal line meets the graph at three points, so there are 3 distinct real roots. If k=0 or k=4, it touches at one point, so there are 2 distinct real roots (k=0: 0, 3 / k=4: 1, 4), and if k<0 or k>4, there is 1.

y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that read that the horizontal line must be between the local minimum value and the local maximum value to meet at three points.
y-m-63-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment that read the range where there is 1 root as the range where there are 3.
